strengths: The paper addresses a clear and significant practical problem in graph coarsening: enabling adaptive (multi-resolution) coarsening without recomputation and correctly handling heterogeneous graphs, which is a major limitation of existing methods.

The experimental evaluation is extensive and convincing, covering 23 diverse datasets, multiple spectral fidelity metrics, node classification performance across many GNN models, and clear scalability comparisons. The empirical evidence strongly supports the method's practical effectiveness.

The framework is well-motivated and clearly integrates locality-sensitive hashing and consistent hashing to achieve its goals. The theoretical analysis (load balancing, projection proximity) adds soundness. The proposed method is model-agnostic, fast, scalable, and demonstrably suitable for real-world graph types.

The paper makes its contribution concrete by demonstrating the method's superiority over a large suite of baselines, including on large-scale graphs where other methods fail (OOT). The handling of heterogeneous semantics via type-isolated coarsening is a crucial and well-validated contribution.
weaknesses: The core adaptive mechanism (merging a random node with its clockwise neighbor in a sorted list) is simple, and the novelty is more in the combination of LSH and CH for this specific purpose rather than a fundamentally new algorithm. The theoretical guarantee on load balance is a nice addition but the mechanism itself is heuristic.

While the paper is generally clear, some parts could be more concise (e.g., the appendix material is very long). The description of the framework in sections 3.1 and 3.2 could be streamlined further for quicker comprehension.

target_paper_summary.title: Spider: Boosting Blind Face Restoration Via Simultaneous Prior Injection And Degradation Removal
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Existing blind face restoration (BFR) methods suffer from drastic performance drop 2 under severe degradations. A common strategy is to first remove degradations and 3 then restore the face by fully harnessing generative prior. However, this sequential 4 pipeline risks discarding subtle but crucial cues from already limited low-quality 5 (LQ) inputs. To address this, we ingeniously introduce a new learning paradigm: 6 simultaneous prior injection and degradation removal (SPIDER). Unlike existing 7 approaches, SPIDER injects semantic prior before degradation removal, thereby 8 preserving identity-relevant features and mitigating the impact of corrupted LQ 9 features. SPIDER consists of two key modules: (1) a prior injection module that 10 distills purified degradation-unaware semantic control tokens from vision-language 11 models, and (2) a degradation removal module equipped with an image-to-text 12 degradation mapper and a degradation remover that refines distorted features into 13 robust representations. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world 14 datasets, including challenging surveillance scenarios, demonstrate SPIDER's clear 15 superiority over state-of-the-art BFR methods. 17 Blind Face Restoration (BFR) is a challenging task that aims to recover high-quality (HQ) face 18 images from low-quality (LQ) ones that suffer from unknown and complex degradations such as low 19 resolution [3, 6], blur [48], noise [13, 28], and JPEG compression [5]. This is an inherently ill-posed 20 problem as the information loss caused by the degradations leads to an overwhelming number of 21 plausible HQ solutions consistent with the same LQ input. To mitigate the ill-posedness, recent 22 studies have explored various prior-based methods to produce high-fidelity outputs. 23 As illustrated in Figure 1, existing prior-based BFR methods fall into three main paradigms: 1) 24 Continuous generative prior (e.g., GFPGAN [36], which learns accurate latent codes via GAN inver25 sion to reconstruct HQ faces with high fidelity; 2) Discrete generative prior (e.g., Codeformer [52], 26 DAEFR [30]), which uses vector quantization to map degraded inputs into semantic tokens and 27 harness a fixed HQ codebook for high-quality restoration; and 3) Diffusion-based conditional genera28 tion (e.g., DiffBIR [18], FaithDiff [2]), which reframes the restoration into conditional generation 29 employing the powerful expressiveness of diffusion prior to achieve significant improvement

target_paper_summary.title: Inconsistency-Aware Minimization: Improving Generalization With Unlabeled Data
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Estimating the generalization gap and devising optimization methods that general2 ize better are crucial for deep learning models, both for theoretical understanding 3 and for practical applications. The ability to leverage unlabeled data for these pur4 poses offers significant advantages in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces 5 a novel generalization measure, termed *local inconsistency*, developed from an 6 information-geometric perspective of the neural network's parameter space. A 7 key feature of local inconsistency is its computability from unlabeled data. We 8 establish its theoretical underpinnings by connecting local inconsistency to the 9 Fisher information matrix and the loss Hessian. Empirically, we demonstrate 10 that local inconsistency correlates with the generalization gap also exhibiting 11 characteristics comparable to *sharpness*. Based on these findings, we propose 12 Inconsistency-Aware Minimization (IAM) that incorporates local inconsistency 13 into the objective. We demonstrate that in standard supervised learning settings, 14 IAM enhances generalization, achieving performance comparable to existing meth15 ods such as Sharpness-Aware Minimization. Furthermore, IAM exhibits efficacy 16 in semi- and self-supervised learning scenarios, where the local inconsistency is 17 computed from the unlabeled data. 19 Estimating the generalization gap and developing optimization techniques to enhance performance 20 on unseen data are pivotal challenges in both the theory and practice of deep learning. strengths: Introduces a novel generalization measure, 'local inconsistency', computable from unlabeled data using a single model, offering practical advantages over existing methods.

Demonstrates effectiveness across multiple learning paradigms (supervised, semi-supervised, self-supervised) with competitive or superior performance to baselines like SAM.
weaknesses: The theoretical connection between local inconsistency and generalization (Theorem 1) is presented informally and relies on heuristic assumptions, requiring more rigorous justification.

reviewers.summary_comment: The author did not submit a rebuttal, so the original assessment stands. reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a highly novel and significant contribution. The paper aligns perfectly with a vision of pushing the field forward with bold, unconventional ideas.

weaknesses: The theoretical generalization bound (Theorem 1) is presented as informal and relies on a heuristic assumption (Eq. 13) that connects the loss increase to the KL divergence; a more rigorous derivation would strengthen the theoretical contribution.

strengths: Introduces a novel Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework to adapt knowledge distillation for Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD), a practical but challenging setting.

weaknesses: The paper is very cluttered and difficult to read seamlessly. The text has numerous formatting and equation rendering errors (e.g., many LaTeX commands are not properly rendered, text appears in math mode, figures and tables are referenced within the text in a broken way). This severely hampers clarity and makes proper evaluation of the method's details challenging.

The theoretical assumptions and analysis in Section 3.2 are hand-wavy and lack rigor. Assumption 1 relies on anomalies being 'sufficiently rare' without quantification, and the link between gradient contribution and representation failure is not proven. The use of the No Free Lunch theorem in Assumption 2 is informal and not applied correctly to support the core claim about lack of generalization.
reviewers.summary_comment: The paper proposes an interesting and timely idea: leveraging knowledge distillation for the challenging FUAD setting by introducing a cross-domain framework to reduce the student network's exposure to anomaly patterns. The core intuition is sound, and initial results show promise. However, the presentation is severely marred by poor formatting, making it an extremely difficult read; tables, equations, and figure references are broken. This fundamentally undermines clarity and confidence in the described method. Furthermore, the theoretical justification provided is weak and lacks mathematical rigor. The experimental evaluation, while showing improvements, would benefit from more robust statistical analysis (e.g., error bars, multiple runs). Given the combination of significant presentation flaws that obscure the technical content and the insufficient theoretical grounding, I cannot recommend acceptance in its current form. Major revisions to the manuscript's presentation and a strengthening of the analytical foundations are required.

3.desc: No RAG, 2 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, AI Detector enabled, no author rebuttal

strengths: The paper introduces a novel Cross-Domain Distillation framework for the challenging Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection task, which is the first to apply the knowledge distillation paradigm to this setting.

The methodological design is well-motivated by two key probabilistic and distributional assumptions about normal vs. anomalous data, and the proposed Domain-Specific Training and Cross-Domain Knowledge Aggregation components are logically constructed to address the over-generalization problem.

Extensive experiments on MVTec AD and VisA datasets under noisy conditions demonstrate significant performance improvements over strong baselines, showing robustness in both 'No Overlap' and more challenging 'Overlap' settings.

The paper includes thorough ablation studies verifying the effectiveness of each module and provides insightful visualizations comparing anomaly score distributions and detection maps with the baseline.
weaknesses: The clarity of the paper could be improved; the manuscript contains formatting issues, incomplete equations, and some placeholder text (e.g., 'denft' in Equation 14), which detract from readability and professionalism.

The statistical significance of the results is not reported (no error bars or multiple runs), which limits the robustness of the performance claims, especially given the stochastic nature of domain construction and training.
While the method is conceptually general, experiments are limited to the Reverse Distillation paradigm; validation on other UAD architectures would strengthen the claim of broader applicability.
reviewers.summary_comment: After considering the lack of author rebuttal, my initial assessment stands. The paper's core contribution remains strong: a novel and effective approach to FUAD via cross-domain distillation. The experimental results are compelling, and the methodology is well-founded. The primary weaknesses regarding clarity and statistical reporting were not addressed, but they do not outweigh the paper's significant contributions. Therefore, I maintain my recommendation for acceptance.

strengths: The paper pioneers the application of the knowledge distillation paradigm to the challenging Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) setting, which is a clearly novel and forward-thinking direction.

The proposed Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework is creative and addresses a core challenge (over-generalization to anomalies) in a non-obvious way via domain division, pseudo-normal feature generation, and cross-domain aggregation.

The method demonstrates strong empirical performance, significantly outperforming the baseline and achieving state-of-the-art or competitive results on standard datasets under noisy FUAD settings, validating the potential impact of the idea.
weaknesses: The theoretical grounding, while based on plausible assumptions about anomaly sparsity and diversity, lacks formal proof and could be more rigorous. The reliance on the 'No Free Lunch' theorem feels somewhat hand-wavy.

Some experimental details are light: error bars/statistical significance are not reported, and the choice of hyperparameters (like the number of domains K and the scheduling strategy) is motivated empirically but not given a strong theoretical justification.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper introduces a novel and significant idea: applying and adapting knowledge distillation to the practical and under-explored FUAD problem. The proposed CDD framework is innovative, leveraging domain-specific training and cross-domain aggregation in a clever way to 'fence off' anomaly interference. The core concept is strong and could inspire future work. While the methodology could be more formally grounded and the evaluation could include more statistical rigor, these are minor concerns relative to the paper's novelty and demonstrated potential. The results convincingly show substantial improvement over the baseline and competitive performance against existing methods. The work is timely, pushes the field forward, and aligns well with the real-world need for robust anomaly detection with noisy data. Therefore, I recommend acceptance.

strengths: The method is built on a clear and well-motivated theoretical foundation, with sound assumptions about anomaly sparsity and diversity (Assumptions 1 & 2) that are used to justify the cross-domain design.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on standard benchmarks (MVTec AD, VisA) under both 'No Overlap' and 'Overlap' settings, demonstrating robust performance improvements over strong baselines.

Thorough ablation studies validate the contribution of each proposed component (DST, CDKA) and explore critical hyperparameters (e.g., number of domains K, feature selection strategy), strengthening the methodological claims.
weaknesses: The core idea of reducing interference by partitioning data into cleaner subsets is not entirely new, though its specific instantiation via cross-domain distillation for FUAD is novel. Some aspects of the domain construction rely on confidence scores from a previous model, creating a dependency that could be vulnerable to early learning errors.

The paper lacks statistical significance reporting (e.g., error bars, multiple runs) for the experimental results. While the overall performance trends are convincing, quantitative rigor for variance would strengthen the evaluation.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a methodologically sound and well-evaluated approach to Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD). The proposed Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework is logically derived from clear assumptions about anomaly properties. The experimental work is extensive, using standard datasets and rigorous comparisons, which convincingly demonstrates the method's effectiveness and robustness. The ablation studies are particularly strong, linking design choices to performance. While the overarching concept of handling noise via subsetting has precedents, the specific application within a distillation framework for FUAD is novel and significant. The weaknesses (moderate novelty and lack of statistical error reporting) are outweighed by the strength of the methodological rigor and empirical validation. The paper is clearly written. I recommend acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and challenging problem: Fully Unsupervised Anomaly Detection (FUAD) where training sets contain unlabeled anomalous samples, which is more realistic than perfectly clean UAD.

The proposed Cross-Domain Distillation (CDD) framework is well-motivated and clearly explained, with a focus on reducing the impact of anomalies during training via domain-specific training and cross-domain knowledge aggregation.

The experimental evaluation is comprehensive and convincing, showing consistent performance improvements over strong baselines on standard datasets under both 'No Overlap' and more challenging 'Overlap' settings.
The paper is exceptionally clear, with excellent visual figures (overview, method details, histograms, anomaly maps) that help explain the methodology and results.

The work includes thorough ablation studies to validate the contribution of each component and provides insightful analysis about dynamic domain numbers and pseudo-normal feature selection strategies.
weaknesses: While the method shows improvements, the core idea (dividing data into domains to reduce per-domain anomaly ratio and using cross-domain pseudo-labels) is incrementally built upon the Reverse Distillation paradigm rather than being a radical departure. The novelty, while solid, is more in the careful adaptation and combination of ideas for a specific setting.

The empirical evaluation lacks statistical significance analysis (e.g., error bars over multiple runs) and does not include a runtime or computational efficiency comparison with memory-based FUAD methods, even though these are mentioned as advantages of the KD paradigm. A more detailed practicality assessment would strengthen the case.
reviewers.summary_comment: This paper presents a well-executed and practically valuable contribution. It tackles the important and realistic FUAD problem with a novel distillation framework that effectively mitigates anomaly interference during training. The method is clearly motivated, soundly designed, and thoroughly evaluated. The paper is exceptionally well-written and provides strong evidence of effectiveness. While the core innovation is an incremental but clever adaptation of the KD paradigm to a noisier setting, the practical significance, clarity, and convincing experimental results make it a solid candidate for acceptance. The work provides a useful tool for practitioners dealing with imperfectly curated industrial datasets.
